questions.q: What does a pointer variable store?
choices: The address of a memory location where a value of a specific type can be stored
A copy of the value held by another variable
The size in bytes of another variable
The name of another variable
questions.explain: A pointer variable stores an address. It points to (refers to) the value at that address, which gives you a level of indirection for accessing memory.

questions.q: Which of the following can a C programmer do using pointer variables?
choices: Write functions whose parameters can modify values in the caller's stack frame
Dynamically allocate (and deallocate) memory at runtime when the program needs it
Efficiently pass large data structures to functions
Guarantee that the program never accesses an invalid address
Interpret bytes of program memory in different ways
Make the compiler reject every pointer type mismatch as a hard error
questions.explain: Pointers support pass-by-pointer parameters, dynamic memory, efficient passing of large data, linked data structures, and reinterpreting bytes. They do not guarantee valid accesses: dereferencing a bad address can crash the program. Compilers may also accept mismatched pointer assignments with only a warning.

questions.q: What are the two most common uses of pointer variables in C programs?
choices: Pass-by-pointer parameters and dynamic memory allocation
Loop counters and array indexing
Storing constants and string literals
Speeding up integer arithmetic and comparisons
questions.explain: Pointers are used most often for pass-by-pointer parameters, which let a function modify its argument's value, and for dynamic memory allocation, which lets a program allocate and free space as it runs.

questions.q: When is dynamic memory allocation especially useful?
choices: When the size of a data structure isn't known at compile time, e.g., an array whose size depends on user input
When an array's size is a fixed constant known when the program is written
When a value only needs to exist for a single statement
When you want the compiler to pick every memory address at compile time
questions.explain: Dynamic memory lets a program allocate space at runtime when the needed size is only known then. It also lets data structures be resized while the program runs.

questions.q: Given the declaration `char *cptr;`, what is the type of `cptr`?
choices: pointer to char (`char *`)
char
pointer to int (`int *`)
It has no type until it is initialized
questions.explain: `cptr` is a pointer to char. It can point to a memory location that stores a char value.

questions.q: Because `int *ptr;` and `char *cptr;` both declare pointers, `ptr` and `cptr` have the same type.
questions.explain: They are different types. `ptr` is `int *` (pointer to int) and `cptr` is `char *` (pointer to char). With pointers you have to track two types: the pointer's own type and the type it points to.

questions.q:
What does this declaration create?

```c
int *ptr1, *ptr2, x, y;
```
choices: `ptr1` and `ptr2` are pointers to int; `x` and `y` are ints
All four variables are pointers to int
Only `ptr1` is a pointer; `ptr2`, `x`, and `y` are ints
`ptr1` and `ptr2` are ints; `x` and `y` are pointers to int
questions.explain: The `*` applies to each name it is written in front of. `*ptr1` and `*ptr2` declare pointers to int, and `x` and `y` are plain ints.

questions.q: Write a declaration for a variable named `dp` that can store the address of a `double`.
questions.explain: Declare a pointer with `type_name *var_name`, so here it is `double *dp;`.

questions.q: Which operator, written before a variable name, gives that variable's address (as in `ptr = __x;`)?
questions.explain: The address operator `&` gives a variable's address. `ptr = &x;` makes `ptr` point to `x`.

choices: `ptr` holds the address of `x`, so `ptr` points to `x`
`ptr` holds a copy of the value of `x`
`x` holds the address of `ptr`
`ptr` and `x` are now two names for the same variable
questions.explain: `&x` is the address of `x`. Assigning it to `ptr` stores that address in `ptr`, so `ptr` now points to `x`.

questions.q: A pointer should be initialized to the address of a memory location whose type matches the type the pointer points to.
questions.explain: For example, an `int *` should hold the address of an int and a `char *` should hold the address of a char.

choices: Nothing; any pointer can safely hold any address
The types don't match: `cptr` is a `char *` but `&x` is the address of an int. The compiler may allow it with a warning, but accessing `x` through `cptr` likely won't behave as expected
`&` can only be applied to pointer variables
`cptr` now holds the value of `x` converted to a char
questions.explain: `cptr` should hold the address of a char. To point to an int, use an `int *` variable.

questions.q: It is safe to dereference a null pointer as long as you only read through it and never write.
questions.explain: A null pointer must never be used to access memory, whether reading or writing. Dereferencing NULL crashes the program with a segfault.

questions.q: What does the special pointer value `NULL` represent, and why is it useful?
choices: An invalid address. You can test a pointer against NULL before dereferencing it to check whether it points to a valid location
A pointer to an int whose value is 0, which you can safely read
A random leftover address that the pointer had before initialization
The address of the first variable declared in the function
questions.explain: NULL means the pointer doesn't refer to any particular address. Programmers often initialize pointers to NULL so they can check them before dereferencing.

questions.q: Which test correctly guards the assignment so that it only happens when `ptr` might point to a valid location?
choices: `if (ptr != NULL) { *ptr = 6; }`
`if (*ptr != NULL) { *ptr = 6; }`
`if (&ptr != NULL) { *ptr = 6; }`
`if (ptr == NULL) { *ptr = 6; }`
questions.explain: Check the pointer's own value (the address it stores) against NULL. `*ptr != NULL` would dereference `ptr` before the check, which defeats the purpose.

questions.q: Running `ptr = NULL; *ptr = 6;` makes the program crash with what kind of memory fault? (Give the common short name.)
questions.explain: Dereferencing a pointer that doesn't hold a valid address, such as NULL, causes a segfault (segmentation fault).

questions.q: In the statement `*ptr = 8;`, what is the `*` operator called?
questions.explain: The dereference operator `*` follows a pointer to the memory location it points to and accesses the value stored there.

questions.q: If `x` is an int and `ptr = &x;` has run, then `*ptr = 8;` sets the value of `x` to 8.
questions.explain: `ptr` points to `x`, so assigning through `*ptr` writes to `x`'s memory location.

questions.q: Assume `int x; int *ptr = &x;`. Which statement stores 20 in `x`?
questions.explain: `*ptr = 20;` writes 20 to the memory `ptr` points to, which is `x`. `ptr = 20;` would instead change the pointer itself so that it points to address 20.

questions.q: What does `y = *ptr2 + 3;` do?
choices: Assigns `y` the value that `ptr2` points to, plus 3
Assigns `y` the address stored in `ptr2`, plus 3
Adds 3 to the value `ptr2` points to and leaves `y` unchanged
Makes `ptr2` point 3 locations further along, then copies it to `y`
questions.explain: `*ptr2` reads the value at the location `ptr2` points to, then 3 is added and the result is stored in `y`.
`q = p` makes both pointers point to `a`. `*q = 7` sets `a` to 7. Then `*p` reads 7, so `b = 7 * 2 = 14`.
`*p1 = *p2 + 10` sets `m` to 4 + 10 = 14. `p2 = p1` makes `p2` point to `m` too. `*p2 = *p2 + 1` sets `m` to 15. `n` stays 4.
`*ptr2 = 10` sets x to 10, and then y = 10 + 3 = 13. After `ptr1 = ptr2`, both pointers point to x, so `*ptr1 = 100` sets x to 100. `ptr1 = &y` repoints ptr1 to y, and `*ptr1 = 80` sets y to 80.

questions.q: `ptr2` points to `x`. After `ptr1 = ptr2;` and then `*ptr1 = 100;`, which statement is true?
choices: `x` is now 100, and `*ptr2` also evaluates to 100
Only `*ptr1` is 100; `*ptr2` still gives the old value of `x`
`ptr1` now points to address 100
`ptr2` is set to NULL because `ptr1` took its address
questions.explain: `ptr1 = ptr2` copies the address, so both pointers refer to the same location. Writing through either one changes `x`, and both see the new value.

questions.q: Assume `int *ptr;`. What does the statement `ptr = 20;` do?
choices: Assigns `ptr` the address 20, so it now points to address 20
Stores 20 in the memory location `ptr` points to
Sets `ptr` to NULL
Adds 20 to the value `ptr` points to
questions.explain: Without `*`, the assignment changes the pointer itself. Dereferencing it afterward (`*ptr = 6;`) would segfault because 20 is not a valid address. To store 20 in the pointed-to memory, write `*ptr = 20;`.

questions.q: Assume `int x = 5; int *ptr;`. Which sequences dereference something other than a valid address, so that they may crash with a segfault or write to an unintended memory location?
choices: `ptr = NULL; *ptr = 6;`
`ptr = x; *ptr = 6;`
`ptr = &x; *ptr = 6;`
questions.explain: NULL is never valid to dereference, and 20 is not a valid address. `ptr = x` uses x's value (5) as an address, so the write likely crashes or overwrites some unrelated location. Only `ptr = &x; *ptr = 6;` correctly sets x to 6.

choices: The value 42 is used as an address, so the write likely crashes or overwrites some unrelated memory location
`x` is set to 6
`ptr` stores a copy of 42, and then that copy is changed to 6
C automatically treats `ptr = x;` as `ptr = &x;`
questions.explain: `ptr = x` stores x's value in the pointer, not x's address. The programmer probably meant `ptr = &x;`.

questions.q: If the compiler accepts `cptr = &x;` (where `cptr` is a `char *` and `x` is an int) with only a warning, then reading and writing `x` through `cptr` will behave as intended.
questions.explain: The compiler may allow the mismatched assignment with a warning about incompatible types, but accessing `x` through a `char *` likely won't behave as the programmer expects. Use an `int *` to point to an int.
